explanation: Mixed bag. Its strongest and most repeatable trigger is ' at' in Apache-license boilerplate ('You may obtain a copy of the License at'). It also fires on '$this->db' in PHP, the opening quote of a URL string, decimal points inside numbers, and suffix pieces of journal names or medical terms (Geoscience, Microbe, infarction). These share no single context.

Fires inside first-person or reader-addressed statements about a first impression or reaction, on tokens such as 'At [first]', 'I [was] intrigued', 'It [struck] me', 'Don't [be] fooled', 'may seem', 'can't help [but]' and 'instantly thought'. What drives it is the impression/expectation framing in the context more than the token itself. Neutral factual text gives little.

Fires on middle subword pieces of technical, mostly biomedical words (arthro-pl-asty, aneur-ys-m, Staphy-loc-occus, car-ious, nosocom-ial, s-elen-ite). It also fires on fragments in math and code, such as '\to' in limits, 'arccos', 'Unsafe' in Swift and SVG path letters. Strongest when the token is a non-initial piece of a rare jargon word. Common words do not trigger it.

Mainly fires on tokens that set up a difficulty, negation or contrast in expository text: 'However[,]', 'difficult [to]', 'doesn['t] work', 'there is [no]', 'has [no]', 'avoid', 'prevents', 'may not [be]'. A separate offshoot fires on 'ju'/'Ju'/'jue'/'JU' word starts (juin, jueves, Juergensen, JUAN).

Hard to pin down. It fires on many tokens with no shared features: the age in 'at the age of [ten]', 'Category[:]' in wiki footers, 'in favor [of]', the 's' in '70s', 'the [media]', 'as you might [guess]', '[=] NULL', and others. Possibly the second half of predictable fixed phrases, but that does not hold together well.

Fires at the turn where expository text introduces a limitation or problem after stating something positive: sentence-initial 'Despite'/'Although', the token after 'but'/'however' ('but [it] is relatively weak', 'however, [this] option'), 'a [limited] clinical value', and 'not [working]' / 'doesn't [run]' / 'not [firing]' in Q&A bug reports. Context signalling contrast or shortcoming is key.

Fires on Greek-letter and special-symbol tokens in technical text: LaTeX Greek names after a backslash (\alpha, \beta, \pi, \eta, \epsilon, \pm), Unicode Greek (β, κ, μ), and the © / ')' of 'Copyright (C)' and the § sign. Arithmetic operators and brackets in math get weaker activation.

Mixture. Strong triggers include the 4-space-indented ' def' starting a method in a Python class, 'java.util.[List/Map]' in import lists, 'as [to]' ('choice as to who', 'clues as to'), and middle pieces of unusual names (Klob-uchar, Bhar-ad-waj, Trai Th-uy). These are unrelated.

Heterogeneous. It fires on adjective suffixes in medical terms (transesophage-al, hyperbar-ic), 'principal [component]', method or field accessors in code (FIRDatabase[.database], random[.choice]), format-string punctuation, and assorted phrase completions ('Staff [Writer]', 'refers [to]', 'Lung [Cancer]'). There is no clear unifying context.

Heterogeneous. It fires on the second token of compound terms or set phrases ('Program [Files]', 'television [studio]', '3D [rendering]', 'social [butterfly]', 'c[DNA]', 'Managed[Bean]', 'typename' in templates) and on word-final fragments. This is loosely 'completion of a multi-token unit', but the examples span code, paths, science and prose with no specific trigger.

Fires on the subword token right after an 'St'/'st' or 'Christ' prefix inside a multi-piece word or name: ST[AP], nyst[ag]mus, St[ew], Bundest[ag], Neost[ig]mine, Christ[al]/Christ[ophe]/Christ[y]/Christ[a], St[over], Standard[Error]. The preceding fragment, not the token itself, drives it.

Fires on a token completing a technical or formal multi-token term: 'Sleep [Ap]nea', "q'th [term]", 'analyt[ically]', 'sc[int]illators', 'nan[ot]ubes', 'Member of [Parliament]', 'energy [harvesting]', 'THE [STATE] OF TEXAS'. It also fires on docket-number digits after 'No. 1'. Fairly broad, with weak specificity.

Fires on physics and electrical-engineering terminology, especially electromagnetic and wave concepts: 'electro[static]', capacitance/capacitor, resonance/resonant, piezo-electric/resistive, 'electric [charge]', 'full [width]', quantum, superconductivity. Weaker on related science terms (frequency, magnetic, biomechanical).

Fires on a lowercase 'l' token, usually standalone or right after a hyphen, as in OCR-garbled contract numbers ('HTC71 l-l4', 'W5J9JE-l l') and chemical prefixes ('-l-homocysteine', '-labeled', '21-lbs', 'a lipoxygenase'). The token must be a split-off 'l' piece; other tokens give almost nothing.
